tour.title: Centro Histórico: Pátio do Colégio to the Municipal Market
tour.summary: The whole birth of South America's biggest city in about four flat kilometres — a Jesuit mission hut, a neo-Gothic cathedral, a working Benedictine monastery, the opera house where Brazilian modernism was booed into existence, a buried river, and the market hall where immigrant São Paulo eats.
tour.overviewText:
Most of São Paulo looks like it was born yesterday and intends to look like tomorrow: glass, concrete, a skyline running past the horizon. So the surprise of the old centre is how small it is. Everything that became South America's largest city — twelve million people in the municipality, twenty million in the metropolitan region — started on one hilltop the size of a modest car park, between two streams, where a handful of Jesuit priests and an Indigenous chief agreed to build a mission.

That was 25 January 1554. The Jesuits — members of the Society of Jesus, the Catholic order founded in 1540 to run schools and spread the faith — had come inland to convert the Tupi-speaking peoples of this plateau. The chief, Tibiriçá of the Guaianás, had his own reasons: an alliance with the Portuguese against rival peoples and the French on the coast. The village they made, São Paulo de Piratininga, stayed poor and peripheral for two centuries. Then coffee arrived.

From the 1850s the crop that Europe drank made this plateau rich. Coffee money paid for the railways, the opera house and the mansions; and because slavery was being abolished at exactly the moment the plantations needed more hands, the state recruited immigrants by the hundreds of thousands — Italians above all, then Portuguese, Spanish, Japanese, Syrians and Lebanese, Germans, Lithuanians, Poles. São Paulo became an immigrant city as few places on earth are: the largest Japanese community outside Japan, millions of Italian descent, an Arab-Brazilian middle class that built whole neighbourhoods downtown. You will walk past their handiwork — the market their appetites filled, the theatre their money built, the churches their faith raised.

The twentieth century took the money elsewhere. From the 1960s offices, banks and the wealthy moved south-west, and for decades the streets around Praça da Sé meant decay, drugs and petty crime. That is changing again — buildings reoccupied by housing movements, museums restored, the Anhangabaú valley re-landscaped in 2021 — but it is a contested, unfinished comeback, and the centre is still quieter and rougher than the rest of the city, especially on Sundays.

This walk stays inside the old triangle. It starts where the city was founded, drops to the cathedral square, climbs to a working Benedictine monastery, crosses the opera square where Brazilian modernism announced itself in 1922 and the valley that once held a river, and ends at the municipal market for lunch. It is about four flat kilometres on busy pavements and pedestrian streets, with three interiors to see — give it three to four hours.

Go on a weekday. The museum and the market keep weekday hours, and Sunday is both the emptiest and the roughest day in the centre. Almost everything here is free; the one ticket worth buying is the small museum at the founding site. Late August is winter here — mild and often grey, so a light jacket beats an umbrella you will forget. Keep your bag zipped and your phone out of sight in the square and around the market, and you will have an easy day.

You begin where a city was invented to convert people and end where the people it converted into a new country are eating lunch. That arc is the tour.
tour.difficulty: Easy. About four flat kilometres on city pavements, pedestrian streets and one bridge — no hills, but constant traffic, crowds and some uneven paving. The cathedral, monastery and market halls are step-free inside; the crypt and the valley under the viaduct are reached by stairs.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start mid-morning on a weekday, around 9:30 or 10:00, so you reach the market before the lunch crush and while the museum at the Pátio do Colégio is open — it shuts on Sundays and Mondays. Weekday afternoons work too. Avoid Sunday, when the centre is at its emptiest and roughest and the museum and market run shorter or closed hours. Late August is winter here: mild, often grey, sometimes drizzly.

stops.name: Pátio do Colégio
stops.narration:
You are standing on the exact spot where South America's biggest city began, and it looks like nothing: a small paved square, a squat whitewashed building, a few benches, a couple of office workers on a cigarette break. That is the point. On 25 January 1554 — the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul — a handful of Jesuit priests said Mass in a hut roofed with palm leaves, roughly ninety square metres, and named the place the Colégio de São Paulo de Piratininga. Jesuits are members of the Society of Jesus, the Catholic order founded in 1540 to run schools and spread the faith; these men had walked up from the coast to convert the Tupi-speaking peoples of this inland plateau.

Two names you will meet all over this city were here. Manuel da Nóbrega was the mission's leader. José de Anchieta was a twenty-year-old novice, later nicknamed the Apostle of Brazil — he learned Tupi well enough to write a grammar of it. And the third founder is the one the statues forget: Tibiriçá, cacique — chief — of the Guaianás, whose village stood on this hill between two streams, the Tamanduateí and the Anhangabaú. Without his alliance the Jesuits had no land, no food and no safety. He is buried in the cathedral you will visit next.

Be honest about what was founded here. This was a mission, and a mission is the soft edge of an empire. The Jesuits catechised and settled Indigenous people and also fought the colonists who wanted to enslave them, which is why the settlers ran the priests out of town in 1640; the priests came back thirteen years later. The people they converted did not get their world back.

Look at the building in front of you. Almost nothing of the sixteenth century survives. The first church and school went up in 1556 under Father Afonso Brás in taipa de pilão — rammed earth, clay packed into wooden forms and mixed here with whale oil; two original walls survive inside the museum, one from the 1500s. The Jesuits were expelled from all Portuguese lands in 1759 by the Marquis of Pombal, and their college became the governors' palace, which stood until 1953. What you see was rebuilt between 1954 and 1979 to evoke the old mission, and it now holds the Museu Anchieta: about seven hundred objects, a scale model of the colonial town, and paulistinhas — small terracotta saints made by Indigenous hands under Jesuit instruction, two cultures fused in a lump of fired clay. In the church beside it, in a glass case, is a relic no marketing department could have improved on: Anchieta's femur.

The museum charges R$26, with half-price and reduced tickets; R$ is the Brazilian real, the national currency. It opens Tuesday to Saturday, 09:00 to 16:45, and shuts on Sundays and Mondays, so check the day — Monday is the common trap. The square and the church are free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Museum full ticket R$26, half price R$13 for private-school students, university students and teachers, R$6 for public-school students, seniors and retirees, free for children under seven and for visitors with disabilities. The square and church are free. Prices move — verify at the desk.
stops.openingHours: Museum: Tuesday to Saturday, 09:00–16:45; closed Sundays and Mondays. The church and the square are generally open daily. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: The square and church are level and step-free. The museum has a step or two and some tight rooms, but it also has a wheelchair entrance, an accessible ticket desk, a tactile route and Libras (Brazilian Sign Language) interpreters — ask at reception.
stops.insiderTip: Ask at reception to see the two original rammed-earth (taipa de pilão) walls from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, preserved inside the museum — and find the scale model of the colonial town, which makes the rest of this walk make sense.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the Pátio do Colégio and turn left along Rua Anchieta, then right down Rua Boa Vista. Follow it south for five or six minutes; it runs straight downhill to Praça da Sé, and the cathedral's twin spires stand at the end of the street.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Pedro Angelini from São Paulo, Brasil, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Praça da Sé and the Catedral da Sé
stops.narration:
The word sé means see — the seat, the throne of a bishop — so Praça da Sé is literally Cathedral Square, and it is also the city's zero point. Find the low stone marker set in the pavement, the Marco Zero: from it the distances of every highway leaving São Paulo are measured, and the house numbers of every street in the city count outward. If you get lost later, remember you started at the point all São Paulo is measured from.

The square itself is about 47,000 square metres of palms, fountains and people — vendors, office workers, students, missionaries, a queue for the metro, someone selling phone cases. It has been the stage for the country's arguments. In April 1984 it filled for Diretas Já — 'Direct Elections Now' — the movement that demanded Brazilians be allowed to vote directly for president as the military dictatorship that had ruled since 1964 came apart. Politics still happens here; so do pickpockets. Phone in a front pocket, bag zipped, and you are fine.

Now look up. This is the Catedral Metropolitana de Nossa Senhora da Assunção e São Paulo, seat of the Catholic archbishop of São Paulo and one of the largest neo-Gothic churches anywhere. Neo-Gothic means the nineteenth- and twentieth-century revival of the medieval pointed-arch style — here, honestly, a Gothic skin over a concrete-and-marble body. The German architect Maximilian Emil Hehl designed it in 1912; the old colonial cathedral on this site was demolished in 1911 and the new one begun in 1913. It was consecrated in 1954 for the city's fourth centenary, with the towers still unfinished — they were finished only in 1967.

The numbers are absurd and true. A hundred and eleven metres long. Spires ninety-two metres high. Room for eight thousand people. More than eight hundred tonnes of rare marble. The dome is not Gothic at all but a version of Florence's Renaissance dome. Look at the capitals along the columns: the carvers filled them with Brazilian produce — coffee branches, pineapples, armadillos — a young nation's joke about who actually paid for this. In the crossing sits an organ of twelve thousand pipes, and the east tower holds a carillon of sixty-one bells — a tuned set played from a keyboard — cast in the Netherlands in 1959, the largest in South America.

Down in the crypt, under the high altar, are the tombs of the city's bishops and two laymen: Diogo Feijó, who governed Brazil as regent while Emperor Pedro II was a child, and Tibiriçá, the chief who let the Jesuits stay. That is the whole history of this city in one room — the Church, the State, and the man whose land it had been.

Entry is free, and this is a working church, not a museum: roughly Monday to Friday 08:00–19:00, Saturday 08:00–17:00, Sunday 08:00–18:00, but closed to visitors during Mass — Monday to Saturday at noon, Sunday at 09:00, 11:00 and 16:00. Hours shift with the liturgical calendar, so verify at the door. Shoulders and knees covered, hats off, voices low.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter. It is an active parish church, not a ticketed monument. Donations for upkeep are welcome but never required; the crypt is normally open with the church.
stops.openingHours: Roughly Monday to Friday 08:00–19:00, Saturday 08:00–17:00, Sunday 08:00–18:00, but closed to visitors during Mass (Monday to Saturday 12:00; Sunday 09:00, 11:00 and 16:00). Hours move with the liturgical calendar — verify at the door.
stops.accessibility: The square is level with wide pavements and the cathedral floor is level and step-free. The crypt is reached by steps or a ramp — ask at the door. Crowds and the square's gentle slopes are the real obstacle.
stops.insiderTip: Go down into the crypt, under the high altar. It is easy to miss and it holds the tombs of the city's archbishops, the regent Diogo Feijó and the Indigenous chief Tibiriçá — the whole city's history in one room.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross Praça da Sé to its northern side and walk up Rua Boa Vista for about ten minutes; you pass the old Banespa tower on your right. The street climbs to Largo São Bento, and the monastery's dark neo-Romanesque bulk sits across the square.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Mosteiro de São Bento
stops.narration:
You have walked from the city's founding to its cathedral; now climb to its oldest continuous institution. The Mosteiro de São Bento — the Monastery of Saint Benedict — has stood on this spot since 14 July 1598, when the land was granted to a Benedictine monk named Mauro Teixeira, a disciple of Anchieta's. Benedictines are the oldest monastic order in the Western Church, living by the Rule written by Saint Benedict in the sixth century, whose motto is ora et labora: pray and work. About forty-five monks live here today. They are not a museum exhibit; they run a school, a philosophy faculty and this monastery, and they sing.

The building is younger than the community. The colonial church was demolished and the present basilica built between 1910 and 1922, designed by the German architect Richard Berndl in a heavy neo-Romanesque style — rounded arches, thick walls, dark stone. The interior was decorated by a Dutch monk, Adelbert Gresnicht, who came from Maredsous Abbey in Belgium and belonged to the Beuron Art School, a movement that held sacred art should be built on mathematical proportion so that geometry itself becomes prayer. Whether or not you buy that, the effect is severe and beautiful: a nave of cool grey stone, stained glass by Gresnicht himself, and a high altar of marble from Italy's Lake Maggiore.

If you can, time your visit to a service. The monks sing the Divine Office — the Liturgy of the Hours, the cycle of psalms and readings that structures a monastic day — several times daily, and they celebrate Mass Monday to Friday at 07:00 and 13:00, Saturday at 05:50, and Sunday at 08:00 and 10:00. The 10:00 Sunday Mass is the famous one: conventual Mass with Gregorian chant, the unaccompanied Latin plainchant of the medieval Church, sung by the monks in the choir. It is the most celebrated liturgy in the city, and it is free — this is a church, not a show. Vespers comes in the late afternoon and the times are posted at the door. Verify all of it: liturgy times move with the season.

Then go to the shop. Since 1999 the monks have sold breads, cakes, biscuits and jams made to recipes that sat in the abbey archive for centuries — the pão de São Bento is the local obsession, and buying it is a small way of supporting a community that has outlasted every government in this city's history. Behind the walls there is also a library of more than a hundred thousand volumes, one of the oldest in São Paulo, including six incunabula — books printed before 1501 — the oldest a New Testament from 1496. You cannot browse it, but you can know it is there.

One story to carry out. In 1641, after Portugal broke free of Spain, a faction of São Paulo settlers refused to recognise the new king and offered one of their own, Amador Bueno, the crown of an independent São Paulo. He refused and ran to this monastery for protection, and the monks calmed the crowd. The city's one chance at being a kingdom ended in a monastery corridor.

Entry is free. Opening is roughly Monday to Friday 06:00–18:00, and shorter at weekends with a midday break; check at the gate. Sunday morning is the one time you should come even if you normally avoid churches.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry to the basilica and the monastery shop. It is a working monastery, not a ticketed site; donations are welcome but never required.
stops.openingHours: Roughly Monday to Friday 06:00–18:00; shorter weekend hours with a midday break. Mass Monday to Friday 07:00 and 13:00, Saturday 05:50, Sunday 08:00 and 10:00 (the 10:00 Sunday Mass is sung with Gregorian chant); Vespers in the late afternoon. Verify — times shift with the season.
stops.accessibility: A short flight of steps up from the pavement into the basilica, then a level nave. No lift to the upper areas. The square outside is level.
stops.insiderTip: Come for the 10:00 Sunday Mass if you can — Gregorian chant, sung by the monks themselves. On any day, go to the monks' shop for the pão de São Bento before it sells out.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the monastery, cross Largo São Bento and take Rua Líbero Badaró south-east for about eight hundred metres, downhill. The theatre's pale facade and statue-crowned roofline close the far end of the street at Praça Ramos de Azevedo.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rodrigo Soldon from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Theatro Municipal and Praça Ramos de Azevedo
stops.narration:
Everything on this square is a boast, and the boast is coffee. In the 1890s São Paulo was getting rich faster than almost any city on earth, and rich cities build opera houses. This one opened on 12 September 1911 — a night late, because the scenery was stuck on tour in Argentina — and twenty thousand people came just to look at the electric lights on the facade. The Theatro Municipal was designed by the Italian architect Cláudio Rossi with drawings by Domiziano Rossi and built by the office of Ramos de Azevedo, the engineer-architect whose name is on half of old São Paulo. Its style is eclectic — the nineteenth-century habit of mixing every historical style at once — with Renaissance and eighteenth-century Baroque outside and Art Nouveau — the whiplash-curve style of around 1900 — inside. The Paris Opera was the model. The square you are standing on, Praça Ramos de Azevedo, is named for the builder and carries his monument.

But the reason this building matters to Brazilian culture is a single week in February 1922. From 11 to 18 February the Theatro Municipal hosted the Semana de Arte Moderna — Modern Art Week — an exhibition in the foyer plus three evenings of music, poetry and lectures, on the 13th, 15th and 17th. The line-up reads like a who's who of everything Brazilian culture did next: the writers Mário de Andrade and Oswald de Andrade, the painter Anita Malfatti, the composer Heitor Villa-Lobos, the sculptor Víctor Brecheret, the painter Di Cavalcanti. Tarsila do Amaral, whose paintings are reproduced on every tote bag in the city today, was in Europe and missed it.

What were they doing? Breaking with the habit of copying Europe. Brazilian modernism insisted that this country's own mixture — its African, Indigenous, immigrant and backland cultures — was material for serious art, not folklore. The press howled. Audiences booed. Malfatti's paintings were mocked as the work of a madwoman. Within a decade the mockers were the ones being forgotten. Every Brazilian who has argued about national identity since has been arguing with that week.

The building has kept up. It has hosted Enrico Caruso, Maria Callas, Vaslav Nijinsky, Rudolf Nureyev and Ella Fitzgerald, and between 2008 and 2011 it was restored from top to bottom, including more than fourteen thousand pieces of stained glass. Today it is home to the city's symphony orchestra, its lyric chorus and its ballet company. Guided visits to the gilded foyer and the auditorium are usually offered but must be booked in advance; if you have not booked, you can normally still walk into the foyer during box-office hours — roughly Monday to Friday 09:00–19:00, weekends 10:00–16:20 — and look up at the grand staircase. Performance tickets cost whatever the programme costs, and a cheap seat in this room is one of the better cultural bargains in South America. Verify the times at the door.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The foyer and public areas are normally free to look into during box-office hours; guided visits are free but must be booked in advance. Performance tickets are priced by programme. Verify at the box office.
stops.openingHours: Box office and foyer visits roughly Monday to Friday 09:00–19:00, weekends 10:00–16:20. Guided visits must be booked in advance. Performance times vary — verify at the door.
stops.accessibility: Level pavements and a step-free square. Inside, the foyer and auditorium involve stairs, but there is a lift — ask staff for the step-free route.
stops.insiderTip: If you have not booked a guided visit, walk into the foyer during box-office hours and look up at the grand staircase and the Art Nouveau decoration — it is free and takes five minutes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk to the far side of Praça Ramos de Azevedo and step onto the Viaduto do Chá — the bridge begins right there, a two-minute walk. Stop at the middle of the span for the view up and down the valley.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Viaduto do Chá and Vale do Anhangabaú
stops.narration:
Stand at the middle of the bridge and look down. This valley had a river in it. The Anhangabaú ran between two hills — the one the Jesuits took and the one the coffee millionaires took — and its name comes from Tupi: anhangá was a white, deer-like spirit with eyes of fire, protector of the hunt and the fish, which Portuguese missionaries helpfully recast as the devil. Other readings say the water itself was the problem, irony and acid, 'bad water'. Either way it was a boundary. The river was channelled and then buried under concrete in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the valley became the seam between what São Paulo calls the Centro Velho, the Old Centre, behind you, and the Centro Novo, the New Centre, on the far side.

The bridge you are standing on is the Viaduto do Chá — the Tea Viaduct — and it was the first viaduct in the city. The name comes from the Morro do Chá, Tea Hill, the slope beyond, where black tea was grown in the nineteenth century; because the plant came from India, then a British possession, locals called it chá-da-índia, Indian tea. Before the bridge, crossing meant a long crawl down and up the ravine. A French immigrant named Jules Martin proposed the crossing in 1877; work finally began in 1888 and stopped a month later, when the Baron of Tatuí sued to save the mansion that stood in the way. The city won, and a crowd with pickaxes demolished the house the same day the verdict came down. The iron span was ordered from a German firm in Duisburg, arrived in 1890, opened on 6 November 1892, and charged a toll of sixty réis — an old Portuguese coin — to cross. The iron version was replaced by the concrete one under your feet in 1939.

Now turn and look along the valley. Those three fountains and twelve sculptures of marble, bronze and granite make up the Vale do Anhangabaú, 43,000 square metres that São Paulo uses as its front lawn and its protest ground. On 16 April 1984 this space held the biggest political rally in Brazilian history: Diretas Já, the campaign for direct presidential elections as the military dictatorship that had ruled since 1964 was collapsing. Organisers and police counted about 1.5 million people. Every government since has used the valley for something — concerts, festivals, the twenty-four-hour Virada Cultural arts marathon — and every government has promised to fix it.

Read the skyline while you are up here. The slender tower flying a flag is the Altino Arantes building, the old state bank headquarters, once the tallest in the city. The one with the clock is the Martinelli, the first skyscraper. The big blocky one at the far end is the Matarazzo building, now the city hall. And under the bridge, behind the Prestes Maia Gallery, are the first escalators São Paulo ever installed. The valley is free and open at all hours, and the middle of this bridge is the best free viewpoint in the old centre.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open access at all hours. It is a public bridge and square, not a ticketed site.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in daylight; after dark the valley is lit but emptier, and it is not the place for a late solo stroll.
stops.accessibility: The viaduct pavements are level but narrow and busy. The valley below is reached by long flights of stairs, so the valley floor itself is not step-free from the bridge.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the middle of the viaduct and look south-east for the Altino Arantes and Martinelli towers, then down at the three fountains in the valley — the best free view in the old centre.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the north end of the viaduct, take Rua Direita east through the pedestrian heart of the old centre, then follow the crowds and the downhill flow toward Rua da Cantareira and the market. It is about a kilometre and a half, twenty minutes on foot. The metro will not help: São Bento station is the nearest, still a ten-minute walk away, so walk it — but stay on the busy streets.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Mercado Municipal (Mercadão)
stops.narration:
Lunch. The Mercado Municipal — everyone calls it the Mercadão, the Big Market — opened on 25 January 1933, the city's birthday, and it is the best single place in São Paulo to understand what immigration did to this city's stomach. The building was designed by the engineer Felisberto Ranzini, from Ramos de Azevedo's office — the same office that built the theatre you just left — in an eclectic style with a German-influenced modular plan drawn up in Germany and modelled on Berlin's central market. Its first job, in fact, was not food at all: it went up as a gunpowder and munitions store, and only after the Constitutionalist Revolution of 1932 — São Paulo's failed uprising against the federal government — could it take over as the city's market, replacing the old open-air market on Rua 25 de Março.

Look up before you eat. The hall is lit by fifty-five stained-glass windows made by Conrado Sorgenicht Filho, a German-Brazilian artist who also worked on the cathedral you saw this morning and on more than three hundred Brazilian churches. They show food production — harvesting, herding, hauling — so the light falling on the fruit stalls is coloured by the labour that produced them. Skylights flood the rest. The hall is 12,600 square metres, with about 290 stalls, roughly 1,500 people working here, some 350 tonnes of food moving through a day, and something like 50,000 visitors a week.

Now the eating. Two things made this place famous. The first is the sanduíche de mortadela, the mortadella sandwich — mortadella being the finely ground Italian pork sausage studded with fat — served here in a version the size of your head. It was born at Bar do Mané, a counter opened in 1933 by two cousins of Portuguese descent; the story goes that in the 1960s the staff built an absurdly overfilled sandwich as a joke, customers demanded it, and a São Paulo icon was born. The second is the pastel de bacalhau: a thin, deep-fried pastry filled with a mash of bacalhau, salt cod, the dried fish Portuguese cooking brought to Brazil and never let go. Both are tourist food, both are genuinely good, and both are priced for tourists — a mortadella sandwich runs somewhere around R$30 to R$50, the pastel around R$20 to R$30, with R$ the Brazilian real. Verify at the counter; prices here move.

Beyond the counters, buy fruit you cannot name. The Amazon arrives on these tables: cupuaçu, a tart relative of cacao; graviola, or soursop; açaí in its unsweetened form; plus cashews, peppers, cheeses and every spice in the Brazilian repertoire. Retail hours are Monday to Saturday 06:00–18:00, and Sundays and holidays 06:00–16:00, though individual stalls keep their own hours and the mezzanine restaurants run later. Entry is free; you pay only for what you eat.

One practical warning. The streets between here and Rua 25 de Março, and Parque Dom Pedro II on the far side, are the roughest stretch on this walk — busy, poor and thick with pickpockets. Walk in and out on the main roads, keep your phone away, and if the pavement empties out, take a taxi.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay only for what you eat or buy. A mortadella sandwich is roughly R$30–50 and a pastel de bacalhau roughly R$20–30, but prices move — verify at the counter.
stops.openingHours: Retail: Monday to Saturday 06:00–18:00; Sundays and holidays 06:00–16:00. Individual stalls and the mezzanine restaurants keep their own hours — verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: Level floor throughout the hall, with lifts to the mezzanine restaurants. Entrances have small steps and the busiest aisles are tight when crowded.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the ground-floor crush and take your sandwich up to the mezzanine, where you can eat looking down through the coloured light of the stained glass. Go on a weekday morning: on Sunday afternoons the market half-shuts and the surrounding streets empty out.
stops.nextStopDirections: That is the walk: a mission hut, a cathedral, a monastery, an opera house, a buried river and a market hall, all inside about four kilometres of the same hill the city started on. Get a mortadella sandwich and a pastel de bacalhau, carry them up to the mezzanine and eat looking down at the stained glass. When you are done, São Bento metro station is a ten-minute walk west and one stop from Sé on the Blue Line; the Museu da Língua Portuguesa, in the old Luz railway station, is one more stop north if you still have appetite for culture. After this much food, a nap is also a legitimate plan.
